Caddy is an extensible server platform written in Go.

At its core, Caddy merely manages configuration. Modules are plugged
in statically at compile-time to provide useful functionality. Caddy's
standard distribution includes common modules to serve HTTP, TLS,
and PKI applications, including the automation of certificates.

To run Caddy, use:

	- 'caddy run' to run Caddy in the foreground (recommended).
	- 'caddy start' to start Caddy in the background; only do this
	  if you will be keeping the terminal window open until you run
	  'caddy stop' to close the server.

When Caddy is started, it opens a locally-bound administrative socket
to which configuration can be POSTed via a restful HTTP API (see
https://caddyserver.com/docs/api).

Caddy's native configuration format is JSON. However, config adapters
can be used to convert other config formats to JSON when Caddy receives
its configuration. The Caddyfile is a built-in config adapter that is
popular for hand-written configurations due to its straightforward
syntax (see https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile). Many third-party
adapters are available (see https://caddyserver.com/docs/config-adapters).
Use 'caddy adapt' to see how a config translates to JSON.

For convenience, the CLI can act as an HTTP client to give Caddy its
initial configuration for you. If a file named Caddyfile is in the
current working directory, it will do this automatically. Otherwise,
you can use the --config flag to specify the path to a config file.

Some special-purpose subcommands build and load a configuration file
for you directly from command line input; for example:

	- caddy file-server
	- caddy reverse-proxy
	- caddy respond

These commands disable the administration endpoint because their
configuration is specified solely on the command line.

`caddy resource validate` prints, and exits with status 1 when `valid` is false:
```json
{"valid": false, "errors": [{"code": "unknown_column", "resource": "Book", "pointer": "/properties/author", "message": "column \"author\" is not returned by the query", "hint": "Query returns: id, title, author_name. Alias the column in the SELECT (expr AS author) or rename the property. see: caddy resource guide queries"}], "warnings": []}
`resource` is the definition `name` (the file name when the name is unknown), `pointer` is a JSON pointer into that definition. `warnings` do not make the definitions invalid: they are served, and the warnings are also logged by the server. Checks run in this order: JSON syntax / TypeScript compilation, schema, identifier, `table` and/or `query`, query, command and handler files and their exports,
Every framework error carries `code`, `message`, `hint` and often `pointer`; the `hint` ends with `see: caddy resource guide <topic>`, the topic that explains the fix. Response bodies: topic `formats`.
## Error codes
| Code | HTTP | When | Fix | Topic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
{{range .Codes}}| `{{.Code}}` | {{.Status}} | {{.Summary}} | {{.Fix}} | `{{.Topic}}` |
{{end}}
Validation codes appear in the report; if they happen at request time (a query failing for a given header value, a fetch denied) they are returned as an error with the listed status. Codes chosen with `ctx.reject({code})` are not listed here.

# caddy resource: agent guide

This binary is the Caddy web server with one extra HTTP handler, `resource`. You declare **resources**, one definition file per resource (JSON or TypeScript) in a directory; each becomes a REST endpoint over PostgreSQL:

- `GET <path>`: paginated collection. `GET <path>/<identifier>`: one item. `POST <path>`: create. `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE <path>/<identifier>`.
- Output is JSON-LD/Hydra by default, or plain JSON, or CSV (`Accept`, `?format=csv`, `/books.csv`). The JSON list envelope and the error body are configurable (`{"items", "total", ...}`, `{"error": "..."}`, topic `formats`).
- A resource **reads** a `table`, or a `query` script returning SQL you write (joins, visibility rules, aggregates); the server adds pagination, counts, filters, sorting, item lookup and their 400 errors. It **writes** with generated `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` (table) or a `command` script run in one transaction, where business rules live. Scripts are **TypeScript** (`.ts`) or **Starlark** (`.star`/`.py`, a Python dialect), same `ctx` API.
- Filters, sorting, page size and header checks are declared **parameters**: never parse the query string by hand.
- Reports, exports, actions, a list and an item with different shapes: **operations**.
- `GET /openapi.json`: OpenAPI 3.1 of every resource. `GET /`: entrypoint listing the resources.

There is nothing to compile and nothing to install. This is the core guide: start writing from it, and read a topic (`caddy resource guide <topic>`, index below) when you need its details.

## Workflow

1. Write `./Caddyfile` (or run `./caddy resource init`, which scaffolds it and a working example):

```
{
	admin off
}

:8080 {
	resource {
		dir resources
		dsn postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/dbname
	}
}
```

2. Start the server once, in the background: `./caddy run > caddy.log 2>&1 &` (it reads `./Caddyfile`). It starts whatever the state of the definitions and **reloads `resources/` by itself** within a second of any change: restart it only after editing the `Caddyfile`.
3. Write one definition per resource in `resources/` (`Book.json`), plus the scripts it references.
4. Request it: `curl -s localhost:8080/books`, `curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/books -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Dune"}'`.
5. Read the errors: they teach. An invalid definition's paths answer its validation errors (`500` problem+json with `code`, `pointer`, `hint`, and `errors` listing all of them); other paths keep working. `./caddy resource validate --dir resources --dsn '<dsn>'` prints the full report. Fix errors in order; every `hint` ends with `see: caddy resource guide <topic>`.

## Example

`resources/Book.json`, a table read and written with generated SQL, filtered and sorted by declared parameters:

```json
{
  "name": "Book",
  "path": "/books",
  "table": "book",
  "itemsPerPage": 10,
  "properties": {
    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true, "readOnly": true},
    "title": {"type": "string", "required": true},
    "priceCents": {"type": "integer", "column": "price_cents"},
    "published": {"type": "boolean"}
  },
  "parameters": {
    "title": {"in": "query", "filter": "ipartial"},
    "priceCents": {"in": "query", "filter": "range"},
    "order": {"in": "query", "filter": "order", "properties": ["title", "priceCents"]}
  }
}
```

`GET /books?title=dune&priceCents[lte]=2000&order[priceCents]=desc&page=2` filters (case-insensitive contains, range), sorts (then by `id`), paginates and counts; `GET /books/7` reads one; `POST /books` validates the body (`title` required, `id` read-only) and inserts. To hide rows, join tables or compute values, add `"query": "book.query.ts"`:

```ts
export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
  return ctx.sql`SELECT id, title, price_cents AS "priceCents", published FROM book WHERE published`;
}
```

Return one column per property, named exactly like it; no `LIMIT`, `ORDER BY` or count (the server wraps your query). Writes then need a `command` (or keep `table`, which still generates them).

## Most used keys

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `path` | `Book`, `/books` (items at `/books/<identifier>`). |
| `table` | Table read (and written) with generated SQL; with `query`, describes the table for helpers and writes. |
| `query` | Script returning the SQL that reads (`book.query.ts`, `book.star`). |
| `command` | Script with `create`/`update`/`remove`, run in a transaction. |
| `properties` | Output: name to `{type, identifier, required, readOnly, column, ...}`; types `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, `datetime`, `object`, `array`. |
| `input` | Body accepted by writes, when it differs from `properties`. |
| `parameters` | Query string and header parameters: filters, sorting, page size, header checks. |

42	  "name": "Book",
43	  "path": "/books",
44	  "table": "book",
45	  "itemsPerPage": 10,
46	  "properties": {
47	    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true, "readOnly": true},
48	    "title": {"type": "string", "required": true},
49	    "priceCents": {"type": "integer", "column": "price_cents"},
50	    "published": {"type": "boolean"}
51	  },
52	  "parameters": {
53	    "title": {"in": "query", "filter": "ipartial"},
54	    "priceCents": {"in": "query", "filter": "range"},
55	    "order": {"in": "query", "filter": "order", "properties": ["title", "priceCents"]}
56	  }
57	}
58	```
59	
60	`GET /books?title=dune&priceCents[lte]=2000&order[priceCents]=desc&page=2` filters (case-insensitive contains, range), sorts (then by `id`), paginates and counts; `GET /books/7` reads one; `POST /books` validates the body (`title` required, `id` read-only) and inserts. To hide rows, join tables or compute values, add `"query": "book.query.ts"`:
61	
62	```ts
63	export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
64	  return ctx.sql`SELECT id, title, price_cents AS "priceCents", published FROM book WHERE published`;
65	}
66	```
67	
68	Return one column per property, named exactly like it; no `LIMIT`, `ORDER BY` or count (the server wraps your query). Writes then need a `command` (or keep `table`, which still generates them).

100	# Definitions
101	
102	Every file directly inside the directory whose name ends in `.json` or `.ts` is a definition, except `*.query.ts`, `*.command.ts` (and their `.js` variants), `*.d.ts`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` and names starting with `.` or `_`. `.star` and `.py` files are always scripts, never definitions. Subdirectories are ignored. Name files after the resource (`Book.json`).
103	
104	A JSON definition backed by a table, readable and writable with generated SQL:
105	
106	```json
107	{
108	  "name": "Author",
109	  "path": "/authors",
110	  "table": "author",
111	  "properties": {
112	    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true, "readOnly": true},
113	    "name": {"type": "string", "filterable": true, "required": true}
114	  }
115	}
116	```
117	
118	The same in TypeScript (`Author.ts`). `defineResource` is a global identity function, there is nothing to import:
119	
120	```ts
121	export default defineResource({
122	  name: "Author",
123	  path: "/authors",
124	  table: "author",
125	  properties: {
126	    id: { type: "integer", identifier: true, readOnly: true },
127	    name: { type: "string", filterable: true, required: true },
128	  },
129	});
130	```
131	
132	A definition backed by a query, writable through a command (`Book.json` + `book.query.ts` + `book.command.ts`):
133	
134	```json
135	{
136	  "name": "Book",
137	  "path": "/books",
138	  "query": "book.query.ts",
139	  "command": "book.command.ts",
140	  "itemsPerPage": 10,
141	  "input": {
142	    "title": {"type": "string", "required": true},
143	    "author_id": {"type": "integer", "required": true}
144	  },
145	  "properties": {
146	    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true},
147	    "title": {"type": "string"},
148	    "author": {"type": "string", "filterable": true}
149	  }
150	}
151	```
152	
153	`properties` is the output (what reads return); `input` is what writes accept. They differ here: a book is written with an `author_id` and read with the author's name.
154	
155	A definition may set **both** `table` and `query`: the table then describes the resource (column mapping, relations, `ctx.resource()` helpers, generated writes) and the query reads. This is the usual shape for a real API:
156	
157	```json
158	{
159	  "name": "Book",
160	  "path": "/books",
161	  "table": "book",
162	  "query": "book.query.ts",
163	  "relations": {"author": {"resource": "Author", "column": "author_id"}},
164	  "properties": {
165	    "id": {"type": "integer", "identifier": true},
166	    "title": {"type": "string"},
167	    "priceCents": {"type": "integer", "column": "price_cents"},
168	    "publishedAt": {"type": "date", "column": "published_at"},
169	    "author": {"type": "object", "properties": {"id": {"type": "integer"}, "name": {"type": "string"}}}
170	  }
171	}
172	```
173	
174	```ts
175	export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
176	  const book = ctx.resource("Book");
177	  const author = book.relation("author");
178	  return ctx.sql`SELECT ${book.columns()}, ${author.columns()}
179	    FROM ${book.table()} JOIN ${author.table()} ON ${book.join("author")}
180	    WHERE ${book.column("published")}`;
181	}
182	```
183	
184	`book.columns()` gives `"book"."id" AS "id", "book"."title" AS "title", "book"."price_cents" AS "priceCents", ...`; `author.columns()` gives `"book_author"."id" AS "author_id", "book_author"."name" AS "author_name"`, which fill the nested `author` object (topic `queries`).
185	
186	To expose only some rows, rename a column, compute a value or join tables, use a `query`: `table` alone cannot do any of that.
187	
188	## Keys
189	
190	| Key | Required | Rules |
191	| --- | --- | --- |
192	| `name` | yes | PascalCase, singular: `Book`, `BookReview`. Used as JSON-LD `@type` and in `/contexts/<name>`. Unique. |
193	| `path` | yes, unless `operations` is set | Lowercase, leading slash, no trailing slash: `/books`, `/book-reviews`. Items live at `<path>/<identifier>`. Unique. Reserved: `/openapi.json`, `/contexts`, `/docs.jsonld`, `/errors`. |
194	| `table` | `table` and/or `query` | `table` or `schema.table`. Alone: reads the declared properties (their `column`) from that table. With `query`: describes the table for helpers, relations and generated writes. Writes with generated SQL unless `command` is set. |
195	| `query` | `table` and/or `query` | Script in the same directory, no directory part: `<name>.query.ts` (TypeScript) or `<name>.star` / `<name>.py` (Starlark). Topic `queries`. |
196	| `relations` | no | `{"author": {"resource": "Author", "column": "author_id"}}` (to-one: `column` of this table holding the related identifier) or `{"books": {"resource": "Book", "foreignKey": "author_id", "many": true}}` (to-many: `foreignKey` column of the related table). The related resource must declare `table`. Used by `ctx.resource()`. |
197	| `parameters` | no | Query string and header parameters: filters, sorting, pagination, header checks, handlers. Topic `parameters`. |
198	| `order` | no | Default sort when no `order` parameter is sent: `{"createdAt": "desc", "title": "asc"}`. The identifier is always added last as a tiebreak. |
199	| `envelope`, `errors`, `errorDetails` | no | The Caddyfile options of the same name, for this resource: `"envelope": {"items": "items", "total": "total", "page": "page", "itemsPerPage": "itemsPerPage", "pages": "pages"}`, `"errors": {"error": "message"}` or `"errors": "problem"`, `"errorDetails": false`. Topic `formats`. |
200	| `unknownInput` | no | `"reject"` (default: unknown body keys are `422 unknown_property`) or `"ignore"` (unknown keys are dropped). |
201	| `command` | no | Script in the same directory: `<name>.command.ts` or `<name>.star` / `<name>.py`. Topic `commands`. Required to make a `query` resource writable; replaces the generated SQL of a `table` resource. |
202	| `input` | no | The request body accepted by `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH` (an input DTO): an object of field name to `{type, required, description}` and the input keys of topic `commands`. Without it, the body accepts the properties that are not `readOnly`. For a `table` resource without command, input names must be columns (the generated SQL writes them). |
203	| `readOnly` | no | `true` disables every write (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` answer `405`). |
204	| `formats` | no | Output formats allowed, among `"jsonld"`, `"json"`, `"csv"`. Default: all three; the first one is used when the client expresses no preference. |
205	| `operations` | no | Dedicated endpoints replacing the default CRUD endpoints. Topic `operations`. |
206	| `allow` | no | `{"fetch": ["api.example.com", "127.0.0.1:9000"], "env": ["API_TOKEN"]}`: hosts (`host` or `host:port`) that `ctx.fetch` may call, environment variables that `ctx.env` may read. Everything else is denied. |
207	| `properties` | yes | Object of property name to property. Key order is output order (and CSV column order). **The query must return a column named exactly like each property** (a table resource reads the property's `column`, default its name). |
208	| `itemsPerPage` | no | Default page size, 1 to 1000, default 30. Clients change it only through a `pagination: "itemsPerPage"` parameter. |
209	| `description` | no | Free text, shown in OpenAPI. |
210	
211	Property object:
212	
213	| Key | Required | Rules |
214	| --- | --- | --- |
215	| `type` | yes | `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, `datetime`, `object` (needs `properties`) or `array` (needs `items`). |
216	| `identifier` | exactly one property (at most one with `operations`) | `true` on the property used in item URLs and for ordering. Its type must be `integer` or `string`. |
217	| `filterable` | no | `true` enables `?<property>=<value>` exact-match filtering on the collection (shorthand when the definition declares no `parameters`). |
218	| `required` | no | `true`: must be present in `POST` and `PUT` bodies. |
219	| `readOnly` | no | `true`: output only, rejected in request bodies when the definition has no `input`. Use it for generated identifiers (serial) and computed columns. |
220	| `column` | no | Table column of the property when it differs from its name: `"priceCents": {"type": "integer", "column": "price_cents"}`. |
221	| `computed` | no | `true`: not a table column (the query computes it); `ctx.resource().columns()` skips it. |
222	| `properties` | for `object` | Nested properties, same syntax, in output order. |
223	| `items` | for `array` | One property describing each element: `{"type": "object", "properties": {...}}` or `{"type": "string"}`. |
224	| `description` | no | Free text, shown in OpenAPI. |
225	
226	Any other key is an error (`unknown_field`; the closed JSON Schema is topic `schema`). Types and the PostgreSQL column types they accept:
227	
228	| `type` | PostgreSQL columns | JSON |
229	| --- | --- | --- |
230	| `string` | text, varchar, char, uuid, name, enums, domains | string |
231	| `integer` | smallint, integer, bigint (serial too) | number without decimals |
232	| `number` | integer types, real, double precision, numeric | number |
233	| `boolean` | boolean | `true`/`false` |
234	| `date` | date | `"2024-01-31"` |
235	| `datetime` | timestamp, timestamptz, date | RFC 3339 string in UTC, `"2024-01-31T12:00:00Z"`; input also accepts `"2024-01-31"` |
236	| `object` | json, jsonb, or one column per nested property named `<property>_<nested>` | object, nested properties in declared order; `null` when every nested column is NULL |
237	| `array` | json, jsonb (`json_agg(...)`) | array |
238	
239	NULL is output as `null` for every type. A mismatch is a `type_mismatch` error: change the declared type, or cast in the query (`price::float8 AS price`, `created_at::text AS created_at`).
240	
241	# Queries
242	
243	A query module default-exports a function receiving a context and returning SQL built with the `ctx.sql` tagged template (Starlark: `def query(ctx):`, topic `scripts`):
244	
245	```ts
246	export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
247	  return ctx.sql`
248	    SELECT b.id, b.title, a.name AS author
249	    FROM book b
250	    JOIN author a ON a.id = b.author_id
251	    WHERE b.published`;
252	}
253	```
254	
255	The SQL you return is wrapped by the server, exactly like this (`r` is the alias of your query):
256	
257	```sql
258	-- collection, page N, with ?author=...&order[priceCents]=desc applied
259	SELECT * FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."author_name" = $1 ORDER BY r."priceCents" DESC, r."id" ASC LIMIT <itemsPerPage> OFFSET <(N-1)*itemsPerPage>
260	SELECT count(*) FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."author_name" = $1
261	-- item GET /books/7 (also used before PUT/PATCH/DELETE and to read back after a write)
262	SELECT * FROM (<your query>) r WHERE r."id" = $1
263	```
264	
265	Consequences:
266	
267	- Return **one `SELECT`** (`WITH ... SELECT` works too). No `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`, no count, no `ORDER BY` for the collection: declare parameters and a default `order` instead (the identifier always breaks ties). Without an identifier (dedicated `GET` operations) and without `order`, nothing is added: your query is sent as is (plus `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` for a page), so its `ORDER BY` holds. Once a filter applies, the query is wrapped and its own order is lost: declare `order` on such an operation. A trailing `;` is tolerated.
268	- Return one column per declared property, **named exactly like the property**. Use `AS` to rename: `a.name AS author`. PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lower case: a property `authorName` needs `AS "authorName"` (double quotes); snake_case property names avoid the problem. Extra columns are allowed and ignored. Two columns with the same name (`b.id, a.id`) are an error: alias one of them.
269	- Rows excluded by your `WHERE` exist nowhere: not in the collection, not as items (`404`), and they cannot be updated or deleted (`404`), unless the query shows them in the `lookup` phase (topic `commands`).
270	- Filters and sorting apply to the columns your query returns (`r."<property>"`, `r."<object>_<nested>"`), so joined and computed columns can be filtered and sorted.
271	
272	Request values are strings: cast them in SQL when comparing with non-text columns, otherwise PostgreSQL may fail to infer the type (`query_failed`). Prefer declared parameters (`ctx.get("since")`, typed and validated, topic `parameters`) to `ctx.request.query(...)`, which returns the raw string:
273	
274	```ts
275	export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
276	  const since = ctx.request.query("since");
277	  const cond = since === null ? ctx.sql`` : ctx.sql`AND b.year >= ${since}::int`;
278	  return ctx.sql`SELECT b.id, b.title, b.year FROM book b WHERE b.tenant = ${ctx.request.header("x-tenant")} ${cond}`;
279	}
280	```
281	
282	## Nested output
283	
284	An `object` property is filled from a json column of its name, or from columns named `<property>_<nested>` (`author_id`, `author_name` fill `author: {"id", "name"}`; all NULL gives `null`). An `array` property is filled from a json column, typically a `json_agg` subquery:
285	
286	```sql
287	SELECT a.id, a.name,
288	  (SELECT coalesce(json_agg(json_build_object('id', b.id, 'title', b.title) ORDER BY b.id), '[]')
289	   FROM book b WHERE b.author_id = a.id AND b.published) AS books
290	FROM author a
291	```
292	
293	Values inside json are converted to the declared nested types (dates, datetimes in UTC, integers).
294	
295	## SQL helpers: `ctx.resource(name)`
296	
297	`ctx.resource("Book")` returns a helper for a definition with a `table`. Everything it returns is a SQL fragment to interpolate in `ctx.sql`: identifiers are quoted and inlined, values are bound, so it is injection-safe.
298	
299	| Helper | Gives |
300	| --- | --- |
301	| `table()` | `"book" AS "book"` (the alias is the table name; a relation helper uses `<alias>_<relation>`, e.g. `"author" AS "book_author"`) |
302	| `alias()` | the alias, as a string |
303	| `column(name)` | `"book"."price_cents"` for a property (its `column`), or any plain column of the table (`column("published")`) |
304	| `columns(names?)` | `"book"."price_cents" AS "priceCents", ...`: the given properties, default every scalar non-`computed` property. On a relation helper, aliased `<relation>_<property>` and defaulting to the nested properties declared for that relation (`author_id`, `author_name`), which fills the nested object |
305	| `identifier(value)` | `"book"."id" = $1` |
306	| `join(relation)` | the join condition with that relation's helper: `"book"."author_id" = "book_author"."id"` (to-one) or `"author_books"."author_id" = "author"."id"` (to-many) |
307	| `relation(name)` | the helper of a related resource, aliased `<alias>_<name>` |
308	| `json(names?)` | `json_build_object('id', "author_books"."id", 'title', "author_books"."title")`, for `json_agg` of a to-many relation |
309	
310	```ts
311	export default function query(ctx: QueryContext): Sql {
312	  const author = ctx.resource("Author");
313	  const books = author.relation("books");
314	  const published = ctx.sql`FROM ${books.table()} WHERE ${author.join("books")} AND ${books.column("published")}`;
315	  return ctx.sql`SELECT ${author.columns()},
316	      (SELECT count(*)::int ${published}) AS "publishedBooks",
317	      (SELECT coalesce(json_agg(${books.json()} ORDER BY ${books.column("id")}), '[]') ${published}) AS books
318	    FROM ${author.table()}`;
319	}
320	```
321	
322	```python
323	def query(ctx):
324	    author = ctx.resource("Author")
325	    books = author.relation("books")
326	    published = ctx.sql("FROM {t} WHERE {j} AND {p}", t = books.table(), j = author.join("books"), p = books.column("published"))
327	    return ctx.sql("""SELECT {cols},
328	        (SELECT count(*)::int {published}) AS "publishedBooks",
329	        (SELECT coalesce(json_agg({obj} ORDER BY {id}), '[]') {published}) AS books
330	        FROM {table}""", cols = author.columns(), published = published, obj = books.json(), id = books.column("id"), table = author.table())
331	```
332	
333	(`publishedBooks` is declared `"computed": true`, `books` as an `array` of objects.)
334	
335	## Queries that return rows
336	
337	When the data does not come from SQL (a remote API, computed values), the query function returns rows instead of `ctx.sql`. The server can no longer paginate or filter for you, so it tells the function what is asked through `ctx.operation`:
338	
339	- `ctx.operation === "collection"`: honor `ctx.page` (1-based), `ctx.itemsPerPage` and `ctx.filters` (object of filterable property to the requested value, already converted to the property type), and return `{ items: [...rows of that page], totalItems: <rows across all pages> }`.
340	- `ctx.operation === "item"`: return the row whose identifier equals `ctx.id` (already converted to the identifier type), or `null` for a 404.
341	
342	Each row is an object with every declared property, values of the declared type (`invalid_row` otherwise). The function may be `async` and `await` `ctx.fetch`:
343	
344	```ts
345	export default async function query(ctx: QueryContext) {
346	  const res = await ctx.fetch("https://api.example.com/quotes");
347	  let rows = (await res.json()).map((q) => ({ id: q.id, text: q.body, author: q.by }));
348	  if (ctx.operation === "item") return rows.find((r) => r.id === ctx.id) ?? null;
349	  if (ctx.filters.author !== undefined) rows = rows.filter((r) => r.author === ctx.filters.author);
350	  const start = (ctx.page - 1) * ctx.itemsPerPage;
351	  return { items: rows.slice(start, start + ctx.itemsPerPage), totalItems: rows.length };
352	}
353	```
354	
355	with `"allow": {"fetch": ["api.example.com"]}` in the definition.
356	
357	## Queries during validation
358	
359	The query function also runs during validation (`caddy resource validate`, startup, every reload) as a collection request for page 1 with an empty request: `ctx.validating` is `true`, no query parameters, no headers (`query()`/`header()` return `null`), no parameter values (`ctx.get` returns `null`), `ctx.filters` empty. I/O is switched off there: when the function returns `ctx.sql`, its columns and types are checked with a `LIMIT 0` query; when it calls `ctx.fetch`, `ctx.db.query` or `ctx.db.exec`, validation stops at that call and checks nothing more, and the rows it returns are validated on each request instead (`invalid_row`). A `ctx.reject` during validation is not an error either: it stops the check. Handlers and commands are never run during validation.
360	
361	# Parameters
362	
363	A parameter maps a query string or header value to the response, declared in `parameters` (per definition, or per operation where it adds to or overrides the definition's by name). The key is the parameter name:
364	
365	```json
366	"parameters": {
367	  "title":         {"in": "query", "filter": "ipartial"},
368	  "author":        {"in": "query", "filter": "exact", "property": "author.name"},
369	  "priceCents":    {"in": "query", "filter": "range"},
370	  "publishedAt":   {"in": "query", "filter": "date"},
371	  "inStock":       {"in": "query", "type": "boolean", "handler": "in_stock.handler.ts"},
372	  "order":         {"in": "query", "filter": "order", "properties": ["priceCents", "title", "publishedAt"]},
373	  "itemsPerPage":  {"in": "query", "type": "integer", "min": 1, "max": 50, "pagination": "itemsPerPage"},
374	  "Customer-Id": {"in": "header", "type": "integer", "required": true, "status": 401, "handler": "customer.handler.ts"}
375	}
376	```
377	
378	| Key | Meaning |
379	| --- | --- |
380	| `in` | `query` (read on collection reads only) or `header` (read on every request of the resource, before anything else). Name headers without the `X-` prefix, deprecated by RFC 6648 (`Customer-Id`): an `X-` header parameter is reported as a `deprecated_header_prefix` warning. |
381	| `type` | `string` (default), `integer`, `number`, `boolean` (`true`/`false`/`1`/`0`), `date` (`YYYY-MM-DD`), `datetime`. Filters default to the type of their property. |
382	| `required`, `min`, `max`, `enum` | Validation. |
383	| `status` | HTTP status of a missing or invalid value, and default status of `ctx.reject` in its handler (default `400`). Parameters with a `status` are checked first: an authentication header answers `401` before the body or other parameters are looked at. |
384	| `filter` | Built-in filter, below. `property` names the filtered property (default: the parameter name), `author.name` for a nested one. |
385	| `pagination` | `page` or `itemsPerPage` (an integer; bound it with `min`/`max`). |
386	| `handler` | Script `<name>.handler.ts` / `.star` / `.py`, see below. |
387	| `description` | Shown in OpenAPI. |
388	
389	Every parameter is parsed and validated before any script runs; a malformed value answers `400 invalid_parameter` (or the declared `status`) with a message naming the parameter, a missing required one `400 missing_parameter`. Undeclared query parameters are ignored. `?page=N` (from 1) always works; a page after the last one returns an empty list. Without a `pagination: "itemsPerPage"` parameter the page size is the definition's `itemsPerPage`. Declared parameters appear in `/openapi.json`.
390	
391	Shorthand without `parameters`: `"filterable": true` on a property enables `?<property>=<value>` exact match; then a query parameter naming a non-filterable property is `400 filter_not_enabled`. Once a definition declares `parameters`, undeclared query parameters are ignored.
392	
393	Built-in filters (the request syntax, then what is added to the `WHERE`):
394	
395	| `filter` | Request | Condition |
396	| --- | --- | --- |
397	| `exact` | `?author=Frank%20Herbert`, several with `?author[]=a&author[]=b` | `= value` / `= ANY(values)` |
398	| `partial` / `ipartial` | `?title=dune` | contains, case-sensitive / case-insensitive; `%` and `_` sent by the client are literal characters |
399	| `range` | `?priceCents[gte]=1000&priceCents[lte]=2000` (`gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`) | `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`; integer, number, date or datetime properties |
400	| `date` | `?publishedAt[after]=2020-01-01&publishedAt[before]=2020-12-31` (`after`, `before` inclusive; `strictly_after`, `strictly_before`) | `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` |
